Which observations help (or hurt) your model's Gini? Gini is usually treated as a single summary metric, but it can actually be decomposed down to the observation level. We can compare each observation to all observations of the opposite class (defaults vs non-defaults and vice versa). The more opposite-class observations it outranks, the higher its contribution. Sum all contributions, divide by 2 (each pair is counted from both sides) → Gini. Where is this useful? ✓ Identify misranked observations hurting model performance ✓ Debug feature engineering and data quality issues ✓ Analyze outliers

Gini = 2 × AUC − 1 In the credit risk literature, this quantity is mathematically identical to the Accuracy Ratio (AR) derived from the CAP curve. This can make the predictive model uneconomical 🚰 and harder to interpret. One solution is pruning entire trees. By identifying and removing trees that deviate significantly from the model’s global mean—those in the "tails" of the prediction distribution—we can shrink Random Forests while maintaining generalization and accuracy. Good point Huy Tran The naïve solution to stabilizing the bins is the Jeffery correction of adding 1/2 to both 0 and 1 outcome, which corresponds to setting a jeffery prior on the probability in each bin. A somewhat more sophisticated solution is to use an hieratical model in which the probability pi of bin i is drawn from a distribution such as the beta distribution. As an added layer, one can also introduce monotonicity, requiring p(i +1 ) >= p(i) (if in order of increasing risk). Such construction means that each bin needs to have enough data to "convince" the model and overwhelm the prior.

I enjoyed the discussions following this post and Andrija Djurovic's one. One comment I'd like to add is about the overfitting phenomena of WoE. I observed that it happens when one categorical feature has many different values. Or even with "discrete" numerical features. As usual, one has to check the stability of the bins through time to see if it makes sense or is just a one-off event.

Good point Huy Tran The naïve solution to stabilizing the bins is the Jeffery correction of adding 1/2 to both 0 and 1 outcome, which corresponds to setting a jeffery prior on the probability in each bin. A somewhat more sophisticated solution is to use an hieratical model in which the probability pi of bin i is drawn from a distribution such as the beta distribution. As an added layer, one can also introduce monotonicity, requiring p(i +1 ) >= p(i) (if in order of increasing risk). Such construction means that each bin needs to have enough data to "convince" the model and overwhelm the prior.

I agree with Gabriel Ryan, FRM on Poisson and NB. They are of course discrete distributions, so that has issues of its own eg the use of a pmf, not a pdf. In theory, one could fit to a gamma distribution, the continuous extension of these; it is closer to NB in that the mean and variance are unequal. But the larger problem I have seen with counts data is the apparent over representation of instances of zero counts. That is, more than eg Poisson would predict. This is an inherent issue in discrete distributions. Rejecting some or all of the zeroes would bias the data, and so is not recommended.
